title: Growing Up Family Memories and Gratitude
transcript: INTERVIEWER: I'm speaking with Sandy Kaiser, who is my grandma. We are recording this interview in Horseheads, New York. Where were you born? SPEAKER: In Elmira, New York, at the Arnado Hospital, which now is only about four blocks from here. INTERVIEWER: What is the worst thing that my mom or dad ever did to me? Yeah. SPEAKER: I was a very quiet kid, so I didn't get in trouble a whole lot. Probably the worst thing was one time when they told me I had to clean my room up and put some clothes away that I just threw on a chair and I didn't do it. And come Friday night when we would go to dances across the street, guess who didn't go? INTERVIEWER: You. SPEAKER: That probably was the worst thing they ever did to me. INTERVIEWER: Can you tell me about your childhood? Do you remember any of the stories they used to tell you? SPEAKER: Oh, I don't remember any stories, but I had a very, very good childhood. I had on my mother's side, I had a set of grandparents. On my dad's side, my grandfather died when I was 8, so I had that grandmother. Our family was very close. I had aunts and uncles and cousins that didn't live around here. They lived one in California, another one in Poughkeepsie, New York. So when they would visit, the cousins, all got together. And it was always everybody together. All grandparents were. If there was a dinner or something, anything going on, everybody went. It wasn't just one set, so. And I was an only child. I wasn't spoiled, except that I didn't have anybody to fight with. And there were kids on our street, so we were all pals together. And most of them, I lived in the Heights, and that's just a small village. And so you knew those kids all the way through graduation. So we always had somebody to play with. So, yeah. INTERVIEWER: What was my mom or dad like growing up? SPEAKER: Oh, just horrible. No, they weren't. They were good. They didn't really give me much trouble. They had to do a couple of little things that you get annoyed with. But they all in all were very good kids. I say I didn't have any trouble with them. If they did anything, I didn't know about it. So that's probably a good thing. INTERVIEWER: Can you tell me the story of when you were born? Can you describe the moment when you saw them for the first time? Saw my parents for the first time. SPEAKER: Saw your parents for the first time, yeah. So when they were born? INTERVIEWER: Yeah SPEAKER: Oh, well, let's see when you. When. Let's start with Ethan's older than you. When Ethan was born, I was there at the hospital with your mom, and you were a cute little guy, and that hasn't changed. And when you were born, I was not there, but I saw you right after you were born, and everybody seemed to be real cute in that family. And when. You want to know about when, Michael, are your dad. INTERVIEWER: Sure. SPEAKER: Well, we didn't. Michael, your dad, and his. Your Uncle Don were twins. And I didn't know there were going to be any twins until five weeks before they were born. So there was kind of a surprise up to that point. But they kept telling me that one of them. They were sure that one of them was a girl. Well, that didn't happen, so. And they were very healthy, and we just doubled up on everything. We didn't have two cribs, two. Any of this. We had to rush out and double up, so. But they were good babies. They were very healthy babies. And that's about it. Yeah. INTERVIEWER: Do you remember any songs that you used to sing to your children? SPEAKER: I'm not a singer. No, I don't. INTERVIEWER: All right. Do you know a story of how our family first came to this country? SPEAKER: I don't know. I only know about my mother's family. My. They are Ukrainian. They came here as teenagers along with their. They each had a brother and a sister, and they came from Kiev, which is not the city that's not. They're having that trouble now. It's called Kiev. Where they came from was Kiev. So quite a bit of that family was here. From there, my father's family were. I don't know where they were born, but they grew up in a farm in Horseheads. And that's all the background I have on them. INTERVIEWER: Good. Do you have a nickname? And if so, how did you get it? SPEAKER: Oh, a nickname. Yeah, just Sandy And it's short for Sandra, I guess, except when my mother would get mad at me and it was Sandra. INTERVIEWER: So what was one of the worst things you ever did as a kid? SPEAKER: Oh, well, when my dad, I. When I was born, my dad was in the service, so. And I don't know, he was in France at some point, and I don't know if that's when it was. So my mother and I lived with my one set of grandparents while he was in the service. My mom worked and the grandparents took care of me. Well, one time, my grandfather. I had to have been around 2 because my dad came home when I was just 2, so I was no older than that. And my grandfather had just painted the living room walls. Well, I picked up a pencil, I was only two, remember? And I took it and I walked all the way the pencil on the wall, all the way around the living room. So when my grandpa come out and saw what I did, it was, you know, why did you do that? I said, I'm writing to Daddy. Well, he said, what am I going to do now? You know, paint the walls? He didn't do anything. And then one time, my grandfather, they were painting the front porch and he left the can of paint open and went to the garage to get something. And when he came back, I was putting dirt in the paint so he could stir it up. That didn't go over real well. But I don't remember him ever doing anything to me, so. But I was just a baby, so, yeah, that was. That was not good. INTERVIEWER: Can you tell me what you did for a living? SPEAKER: I was a secretary. Well, let's see. I worked for a doctor at one time till he retired. And I was not a nurse. I was just worked in his office and did nursing things, but I wasn't a nurse. I worked at what was known as the artistic card company, where probably 90% of the kids that got out of school that didn't go, move away went to work for them. And I was a secretary there. And then I worked for a doctor friend and I was in the office there until he moved away. And my last job was I was a secretary in the guidance office at El Mar Free Academy. And that's where I retired from. INTERVIEWER: Perfect. Did you like your job? SPEAKER: Yes, I did. I really did. One of the questions they asked me before I got hired was, do you like teenagers? I said, well, I like mine. And I said, I think so. I said, they all had good friends and they were all good kids. So I said, that's my experience with teenagers until I get into school. And, you know. So, yeah, I like teenagers. INTERVIEWER: What is your favorite memory of me? SPEAKER: Maybe when you were born, just, you know, just when you'd be. When you'd be around and you're playing and thinking, you know, that's fun to see. Just watch your grandchildren playing. And now you're in hockey and I really enjoy going to those games and watching you. I sometimes miss some of the things that are going on because I'm watching you come up and down. INTERVIEWER: What do you feel most grateful for in your life? SPEAKER: My family and my religious training, which I still I go to church all the time, so I'm grateful for that.

title: A Century of Work and Living Simply
transcript: INTERVIEWER: What’s the secret to working so long and why do you do it? SPEAKER: Well, I like my job. You can’t stay on any job 77 years if you don’t like it. So I got a perfect record. 1934 until today. Missed one day of work. INTERVIEWER: That’s about 72 years. SPEAKER: That’s right. I missed one working day. INTERVIEWER: Now has your job changed a lot since…? SPEAKER:  It’s changed a lot. It’s changed a lot. Job has changed. Managers change. I still stay there. INTERVIEWER: A lot of people wonder how a person lives to be 100 years old… what do you think you did that allowed you to live so long healthy? SPEAKER: We livin’ too fast on junk food. Tastes good. But I don’t fool with it. INTERVIEWER: A lot of people today try to do things to fight growing old and the last time I talked to you, you had made a comment about Viagra. SPEAKER: Awww. No no. INTERVIEWER: You were talking about Viagra. SPEAKER: Hell. You don’t worry about things you can’t do. Don’t worry about it. And trouble of today people seem like they can’t get the… they go to the store and they’re on these talking phones all day and night trying to work and talk on them phones all the same time. Everybody. Kids got the little phones and they’re talkin’. I don’t have one. I don’t need nobody to keep up with me that tight all day and night and I don’t wanna keep up with no body all day and night. INTERVIEWER: Right. What would you like to talk about? SPEAKER: We goin’ to far in life with the credit card. Credit interest is killing ya. People don’t understand that. I don’t have all them credit cards. I don’t have to have all this luxury stuff, if I can’t afford it I don’t bother with it. I can do without it. INTERVIEWER: What do you plan to do after you retire? SPEAKER: You can’t wait till 99 to do hardly anything. See I did a lot of goin’ all the way up. I been all Europe, Asia and all around Hawaii and Bahamas and Puerto Rico and Tahiti and everywhere else. I rode the freight train farther than some people rode inside. Wasn’t scared to go nowhere. INTERVIEWER: Uh huh. That’s amazing to be 100 years old, still working, still in good health, and still smart, bright. SPEAKER:  If I go to think about how old I am I won’t be able to get up in the morning and go to work. INTERVIEWER: Right. SPEAKER: I don’t worry about age. I don’t think about it. Moses and all them other people, a lot of people over there have lived 8,900 years. I think I’d go to live 900 like all the rest of em or something else. INTERVIEWER: Well I know you’ve inspired me and I love you and I think what you have to say is important. You’ve lived in a time, in an era where so much has changed SPEAKER: that’s right. INTERVIEWER: and you’re still here to talk about it. So thank you very much uncle Arthur. SPEAKER: Thank you. INTERVIEWER: Love you.

title: A Lifetime Love Story from Sunday School to 55 Years of Marriage
transcript: INTERVIEWER: Okay, I'm interviewing my grandma Dixie or Dixie McIntyre and I am going to ask her about her love story. So, Dixie tell me about the first time you met Mac, who's my grandpa. SPEAKER: The first time I really met Mac was during Sunday school. We have known each other since the fourth grade and his family went to. My dad was a minister, the Christian church in Midland, Texas. And when his family moved there, they joined my dad's church. And Mac and I went to the same Sunday school class. But Mac was real shy and quiet, but he played the piano. So my first recollection of Mac was a little boy who played the piano but didn't talk very much during Sunday school. But later when we were teenagers, and I think we were sophomores in high school, our youth group went to Carlsbad Caverns and our church had an old school bus. Not air conditioned or anything, just an old school bus. And so the youth group went on this trip of several hundred miles and Mac asked to sit by me on the school bus on the ride there. And then we walked, walked through Carlsbad Caverns together. And we might or might not have held hands. I don't remember. That was a long time ago. And we rode with each other on the school bus back. And that is how we first kind of the first thing we did together. But the next thing we did was he invited me to a football game. And he went to one high school, Lee High School in Midland, and I went to Midland High School. So he came over to get me for the football game. And my dad was working in the front yard and he thought Mac was coming to get my brother. I have an older brother that's just one year older, not me. He didn't know that I had a date with Mac, with Mac. INTERVIEWER: And was it officially a date? SPEAKER: Yes, we went to the football game together and he had a car and he might have been been driving his brother, he has an older brother who had a Corvette, a 1966 Corvette. And you could take the top off. And his brother might have let him. I can't remember to come and get me in that Corvette. And that was just so exciting to ride around in that black Corvette. And we went to the football game and then we basically started dating. And we would go to the picture show or we would go to the hamburger place or drive around. Midland was a fairly small town and so it was just like you see in the movies that people drove around and you never knew who you might see driving around town, going to the hamburger and the malt shops and stuff. And we dated all through high school until our senior year in high school. And I was going to go to TCU and Mac was going to go to Texas. And so he thought it would be best that we kind of quit dating and he would meet some new people going to Texas. And so we quit dating. And I was really sad about that. And we did not go to senior prom together, which was really sad for me. I mean, I had a date and I went to Midland High School, senior prom, and he did too, went to his senior prom. And then when we were at the end of our freshman year, we started writing letters. And actually, Mac, I kept all. And I have all of the letters Mac wrote me while he was in high school. And kind of how we got back together. And not too long ago, as I was cleaning out something, I found the box with all of his letters. Now he didn't keep my letters. So it was a one sided conversation of how we got back together and how finally we started seriously dating and how after our sophomore year in college, he proposed and we got married in his junior year of college. And that will be January, the last day in January of 2024, 55 years that we've been married. And you have to just count the four, five, six years that we dated. So we've known each other a really, really long time. And we're still each other's best friends and still sweethearts. INTERVIEWER: That's lovely. Yeah. And that's the story of how my grandparents fell in love. SPEAKER: Beautiful. And still are. INTERVIEWER: Yeah. SPEAKER: And one of the best, best days was when we had kids. And Cass's mother is my daughter Heather. And Cass was always, she was the oldest and only. And we loved, love, love meeting her mother halfway when she was at least six months old and getting her for the weekend and then we would meet halfway again and pass her back and she would come and stay with us for a week over the summer. And we just adored Cass and now she's all grown up and ready to go to college herself. INTERVIEWER: Yes. Very exciting. Well, thank you, Dixie for sharing. And yeah.

title: Starting Over: A Mother's Story of Choosing a New Path for Her Daughter
transcript: INTERVIEWER: Hi, my name is Bryanah I am 26 years old. It is May 8, 2024, and I am here in Charlotte, North Carolina with my mom. SPEAKER: Hi, I am Babetta Popoff. I am 51 years old. Today is May 8, 2024. I'm in Charlotte, North Carolina, with my daughter, Bryanah INTERVIEWER: Okay, so I'm going to start things off with just this first question here, which is, do you remember what was going through your head when you first saw me? SPEAKER: Yeah, maybe not the very 1st, 2nd, but the first thing that comes to mind when I hear that question is how wise you seemed. You didn't cry. You didn't, you didn't care what the nurses or the doctors wanted to do with you. You just wanted to stare into people's eyes. And I just felt like you knew me right away. I feel like I had a very close friend at the time who came to visit in the hospital, and she had to give you back after holding you for just like a minute or so because she felt like you were staring into her soul. So I just felt like you wanted to be here. You wanted to be here with me as your mom. And yeah, I remember even saying, oh, I hope I have what it takes to be your mom, because I can tell that you have purpose. INTERVIEWER:  I know. I remember some of the sort of stories surrounding my birth story, which is kind of a lot, but are there any sort of like, moments of that that you want, want to sort of highlight here? Because I think that that's sort of relevant to that point as well. SPEAKER: Yeah. So you're right. Your birth was an experience. You were late. You were about two weeks late, two weeks later than they expected you to be. And we also thought that you were a boy. Through my whole entire pregnancy, we had a name picked out and everything, and the doctors were already calling you by the name when I went into labor. I went into labor on the night before we went into the hospital, but I was scheduled to be induced because we were so late. And unfortunately, due to whatever processes were already in place when they induced me, even though I had already started. So that made labor difficult. And at one point in time during labor, we both just kind of said, nope, we're done. And I heard your heart monitor flatline and I heard mine kind of start to go. And then I don't remember much until I woke up and said, you know, I really feel like something's happening here. And I remember the doctor saying, saying, what was your girl's name because. Because you weren't Tyler. And right before I. I guess I passed out or whatever happened when that blip of time happened, waking back up and having you on my chest and the doctor says, everything's gonna be all right, you're just gonna have to start all over from the beginning. Right when they stopped the. Actually, it was before you were even born, when they stopped the inducing and all those kind of things, they got me back to normal. I already been in labor for a while, but basically I was just gonna have to start all over. But that phrase, everything's gonna be all right, you're just gonna have to start all over. I didn't realize it until several years later, but that was almost a redirect just in our life path, because everything was all right, but we had to start all over and we moved on, just you and I. So that was probably very impactful. When I started writing the birth story and looking back on it each year, that's how I realized how impactful that particular moment was. INTERVIEWER: What was that? What was that? Start over. Like. SPEAKER: You were a baby that always had to know where mom was. And at a point in time, as a tired mom, that gets a little hard because I couldn't even go to the bathroom without you just screaming your head off. And there was a point in time when, let's see, June, June, July, July, August, August. So, yeah, you were about seven or eight months old, and I realized that the relationship that I was in with your biological father was just not right. And it was just not going to be good for us. It wasn't good for me, it wasn't going to be good for you. And I decided it was time to go. And like I said, you were a little one who just always had to have eyes on mom. And when I decided we were living in a pretty cool warehouse space that we had turned into an apartment, but it was all open and you could kind of see everything, but he was asleep and you were in your walker, and I kind of grabbed three bags full of things and I looked at you and I just said, shhhh. Because I had to go down three flights of stairs to put all those things in the car and then come back up and get you. And you didn't make a peep, you didn't make a sound, and you were in the exact same spot where I left you, just kind of looking at the door, and I just. Another reason I knew it was right. And I picked you up and I put you in the van and drove off and I looked in the rear view mirror for a few minutes, just waiting for someone to be in the rearview mirror. And every step of the way, once I made that decision, I knew it was right because everything just kept happening correctly. So it was just reassurance. Yeah. A little later on in that experience, I listened to another radio show. And at that point in time, it was a pretty highly religious radio show, because for whatever reason, I was feeling like I needed that in my life again. And although it's probably not what the announcer meant, he was quoting something out of Malachi and said, children need to grow up in the love in which they were created. And I was really struggling with being a single mom and leaving your father. We weren't married, but he was still your father. And that quote hit me, you know, children need to be raised in the love in which they were created. And you were, because I loved you and you were mine, and I knew you were going to be okay. And so those restart moments, little, little glimmers, letting me know that we were doing the right thing and we were going to be okay. And anytime I questioned it or any time I tried to reconcile the relationship or encourage your relationship with your biological father, we ran into. We ran into walls, and I just wouldn't let us keep running into them. So we were on the right track. INTERVIEWER: What was I like as a baby or as a toddler? SPEAKER: Well, as a baby, you were wise. And like I said, I knew that you always wanted to be here. You were also not just wise, you were in tune. You were aware of your surroundings, highly visual, and always on the lookout. Always on the lookout. You went to, I think we called it the butterfly school, one of the little daycares that you went to. And I, for all intents and purposes, was a single mom. We were living with my parents at the time, so I could help take care of papa, but I came to pick you up, and a bunch of moms were also out there talking with the teachers. You are all out playground time, so I wasn't going to take you away from that. And all the other moms had a seat, and I didn't have a seat, and I kind of had you out of the corner of my eye, and you were dragging like a, what looked like a giant duplo block, you know, like those big kids legos. And you were dragging it across the playground, and the playground had all those little rocks, so already not easy for three year olds, four year olds to walk in because they're kind of lumpy. And then you're dragging this chair that really is half your size because you were only three and you made it all the way over to me and you said, here, mom, sit. And every other kid didn't even know their mom was there, and you were worried about whether or not I had a seat to sit in. So you were that kind of, you were that kind of little kid looking out for others, looking out for me. So also very funny. You know, you had certain ways that you pronounced things that made people chuckle. Fruit cup was definitely not appropriate. And then you also, because your grandparents are both deaf, you also really tried to communicate with your hands pretty early on. Might not have always been right, but you always tried. And so toddler Bryanah was happy go lucky and liked to explore because you were aware of all the things around you. You almost kind of called things into being. You would say you would see something like, oh, I wish I had something like that, or, I'd like to find this book, or I'd like to read more about that. And we'd wind up at some of our favorite little thrift store stomps. And all of a sudden, boom, there it was like it was supposed to be.

title: Grandma Linda's Memories of Family Friendship and Making Your Own Happiness
transcript: INTERVIEWER: I am Isabella Richardson and I'm speaking with Linda Richardson, who is my grandmother.So, Grandma, who do you think the most interesting person is in our family and why? SPEAKER: I think Grandpa Tom is the most interesting person because he has had variety of life experiences, both young and as he got older, with a diverse group of people. INTERVIEWER: Okay. What are some of your favorite memories from your childhood? SPEAKER: Spending the summers with my grandparents. INTERVIEWER: What was your favorite thing to do with your grandparents in the summer? SPEAKER: We just kind of hung out, but they lived by a place called Fort Ontario, and we would go play in the fort. INTERVIEWER: Okay. How did you meet Grandpa? SPEAKER: I met Grandpa in college. INTERVIEWER: And what's the story behind you two meeting? SPEAKER: We were in the same chemistry class, but I met him actually in the school cafeteria. INTERVIEWER: How? SPEAKER: I sat down at a table where he was having lunch with his fraternity brothers, and we had a little interaction. INTERVIEWER: Yeah, what was the interaction?  SPEAKER: His fraternity brothers were being really stupid, and so was he. And so I asked him how long you had to eat the food here to become like that. INTERVIEWER: What is your most memorable traveling story? SPEAKER: When we took our family from Springfield to Mount Rushmore, to Yellowstone to Portland, through the Grand Tetons and down to Southern California. INTERVIEWER: Did anything interesting or out of the ordinary happen while you were on that trip? SPEAKER: Interesting. We had never seen Mount Rushmore. On the way to Mount Rushmore, we saw this little tent place, and when we went in, it had all sorts of snakes and other reptiles running around inside it. And Uncle Brian played tic tac toe with a chicken, and your dad put a little chameleon in his pocket and tried to walk out of the place with it. INTERVIEWER: What was the most challenging obstacle you faced in your life? SPEAKER: Leaving my family and moving to a date. Once I got married, where I knew no one. INTERVIEWER: Why did you decide to do that? SPEAKER: Because I got married. INTERVIEWER: What has brought you the most joy in life? Explain. SPEAKER:  The most joy in my life has come from having my children and grandchildren and making memories with them. INTERVIEWER: What are some of your favorite memories you've made with your children and grandchildren? SPEAKER: Different trips that we have taken. Just the special times together, like at the lake or teaching you guys to swim. Things like that. INTERVIEWER: Who was your best friend in your younger years, and how did they change your view of life today? SPEAKER: One of my best friends is my friend Mary, and she's always been a very stabilizing force in my life. Very supportive, very understanding, very giving. And she has shown me the value of true friendship in life. INTERVIEWER: For your great, great grandchildren listening to this years from now, is there any wisdom you'd want to pass on to them? What would you want them to know? SPEAKER:  I think you have to learn to make your own happiness. Even when things seem really challenging. I think you have to have faith. I think you have to have courage. I think you have to believe in yourself. And again, I think you have to make your own happiness. Okay.
